# The Chemistry of Game Design — skill atoms (Dan Cook / Danc, Lostgarden)

- Type: LINK ONLY card (essays © the author; free to read on his site).
- Source: https://lostgarden.com/2021/03/13/the-chemistry-of-game-design-2/ (2021 revision; original 2007: https://lostgarden.com/2007/07/19/the-chemistry-of-game-design/)
- Author: Daniel Cook — veteran designer (Spry Fox co-founder; also the long-running "Game Design Patterns" / game-design-skills writing at the Game Design Skills site).

## The reasoning method, distilled

- **The skill atom is the unit of game design.** One learnable skill, drawn as a feedback loop: the player holds a mental *model* of how the game works → takes an *action* → the *simulation* responds → *feedback* shows what happened → the model updates. Learning (and most of what players call fun) happens inside this loop.
- **A broken stage breaks the skill.** If feedback is slow, hidden, or ambiguous, the player cannot update their model — the game feels random or dead no matter how good the underlying numbers are. If there is no real decision, there is no skill, only waiting.
- **Atoms chain into skill chains.** Mastering one atom becomes the foundation (and often the literal input skill) for the next. Progression design = arranging atoms so each new one reuses earlier mastery while adding one new decision. A game's depth is the shape of this network, not the count of features.
- **Method of use**: inventory the atoms your game actually contains; for each, check the loop's stages for the weakest link; grow the game by strengthening weak loops and adding atoms that chain from strong ones — not by adding disconnected features.

## For みゅけ

みゅけ is mostly a watching game, so its atoms are observational and managerial: "read the bottleneck lamp and pick the fix", "time a cheer/snack", "choose the next research". Each still needs a complete loop — readable feedback on the strip is what turns ambience into a game. See `checklist-skill-atom-loop.md`.
